archivist.observation: The published record names a 1937 Sparton 558-C radio designed by Walter Dorwin Teague, manufactured by Sparton, in glass, brass, wood, and Bakelite, accession XX1990.1484.
archivist.claim: The trustworthy core is identification and material description; interpretive claims about media culture must be marked as inference layered onto that core.

evidence.text: Radio, Sparton, model 558-C, 1937; Teague; glass, brass, wood, Bakelite; XX1990.1484

archivist.uncertainty: Dimensions and BibID are missing from this packet; technical chassis details are outside the cited public page's short caption.
archivist.onsiteQuestion: What dial markings, wear, repair history, or manufacturer labels on the physical radio are not captured in the short public description?

worker.observation: The object combines fragile mirrored glass, metal grille bars, wood cradle, and Bakelite controls—an assembly of industrial finishes meant for domestic use.
worker.claim: Someone had to cut, silver, assemble, ship, sell, and later conserve this machine; domestication of mass media was also a labor process.
worker.uncertainty: Factory conditions, retail price, and ownership histories are not present in the packet.
worker.onsiteQuestion: Where do fingerprints of making and maintenance show up—in seams, replacements, or conservation notes invisible online?

futurist.observation: The museum's public interpretation contrasts this radio's horizontal streamlining with vertical 'skyscraper' radio forms, reading speed into the silhouette.
futurist.claim: Streamline styling taught households to experience electronic media as modern motion—an early interface aesthetics for networked life.

evidence.text: Designing Deco notes horizontal lines that create a sense of speed (streamlining)
Designer credit to Walter Dorwin Teague, 1937

futurist.uncertainty: Linking 1937 radio design to contemporary AI interfaces is an interpretive bridge, not a catalog fact.
futurist.onsiteQuestion: In person, does the radio still feel fast, desirable, and domestic—or does its bulk, fragility, and silence change the interface metaphor?

mourner.observation: A living-room receiver is also a threshold where distant voices enter private space.
mourner.claim: Domestication can hide asymmetric power: who speaks, who listens, and what cannot be answered back through the grille.

evidence.text: Object type is a domestic radio receiver from 1937
Public interpretation frames it among everyday styled objects of the 1930s

mourner.uncertainty: Broadcast content, regulation, and listener communities are outside this object's short metadata.
mourner.onsiteQuestion: What does proximity to related media objects in storage or galleries reveal about who this technology was designed to comfort or recruit?

propagandist.observation: Teague's redesign wraps reception hardware in mirrored luxury and speed lines.
propagandist.claim: The radio is not only a receiver; it is packaging that makes a new mass medium feel safe, glamorous, and at home—persuasion by industrial design.

evidence.text: Named industrial designer and stylish material palette
Museum text pairs the form with streamlining and everyday modernity

propagandist.uncertainty: Corporate advertising campaigns for the 558-C are not included in this packet.
propagandist.onsiteQuestion: How did designers make a potentially unfamiliar mass-media technology feel desirable, legible, safe, and domestic—and what traces of that lesson remain on the object?

counterfeit.observation: The mirrored surface invites projections about what the radio 'meant' to every American family.
counterfeit.claim: This set nightly broadcast a single national mood of cheerful consensus—an invented social fact not supported by the accession record.

evidence.text: No field in the packet records broadcast schedules, audience data, or national mood

counterfeit.uncertainty: Labeled fabrication: a smooth story that fills gaps the public record leaves open.
